summary: Extends the Integrated Services management objects with those specific to Guaranteed Service. It uses SMIv2 and lets network managers inspect how a device provides guaranteed delay and bandwidth.

eli5.summary: It adds extra dials to the control panel, just for the guaranteed-delivery option.

questions: snmp objects for intserv guaranteed service
what is the integrated services guaranteed mib
what is the slack term in guaranteed service
subtitle: SNMP objects that let a manager read and set the Guaranteed Service attributes of each interface.

tldr.problem: Routers that offer the Integrated Services Guaranteed Service need a standard way for network managers to see and configure the per-interface values the service depends on.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2214 defines an SMIv2 MIB module with one table, indexed by interface, holding a backlog term, a delay term, a slack term and a row status.
tldr.outcome: Managers can read or set these values over SNMP. Setting them creates a reservation under rules different from those of an RSVP negotiation.

today: RFC 2214 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the Guaranteed Service MIB module.

sections.title: Where This MIB Fits
sections.content:
RFC 2214 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for TCP/IP networks. It covers the interface attributes defined by the Guaranteed Service of the Integrated Services model.

The document follows the SNMPv2 Network Management Framework. That framework has four parts: the SMI (RFC 1441) for describing and naming objects, MIB-II (RFC 1213) as the core set of objects, the administrative architecture (RFC 1445) and the protocol for network access to managed objects (RFC 1448).
sections.eli5: Network equipment has a standard way to be asked questions from afar. This document adds a new set of questions just for the guaranteed-delivery option.

sections.title: Objects and Textual Conventions
sections.content:
Managed objects are reached through a virtual information store, the MIB. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and the object type together with an instance identifies one specific value.

The MIB also introduces textual conventions. The RFC says these only improve readability: they change neither the syntax nor the meaning of any object, and objects using them are encoded with the rules of the primitive type.
sections.eli5: Every setting gets a unique name tag, like a label on a drawer. Nicknames make the list easier to read but do not change what is in the drawers.

sections.title: The Interface Attributes Table
sections.content:
The module is called intSrvGuaranteed and sits under intSrv as node 5. It has three branches: objects, notifications and conformance. The attributes live in the Integrated Services Interface Attributes Database, which the RFC says holds information shared with other reservation procedures such as ST-II.

The single table, intSrvGuaranteedIfTable, has one row per interface, indexed by ifIndex. Each row has four columns: intSrvGuaranteedIfBacklog, intSrvGuaranteedIfDelay, intSrvGuaranteedIfSlack and intSrvGuaranteedIfStatus. All four are read-create, so a manager can both read and set them.
sections.eli5: It is a spreadsheet with one row for each network plug on the device. Each row has four boxes to fill in.

sections.title: Backlog, Delay and Slack
sections.content:
Backlog is the data backlog that arises because a real implementation deviates from strict bit-by-bit service. For packetized weighted fair queueing it is set to the Maximum Packet Size. It is measured in bytes. An element can advertise a value between 1 and 228, and the total over all elements can reach (232)-1, which is also the cap on the end-to-end value.

Delay is the maximum packet transfer delay through the element, independent of bucket size. It is measured in microseconds, with the same bounds as Backlog: 1 to 228 for one element and a cap of (232)-1 end to end.

Slack is for an element that uses some slack, Si, to reduce the resources reserved for flow i. It must store Si and reuse it, without recomputing, when reservation refreshes arrive. The RFC gives the required end-to-end delay as b/r + Ctot/r + Dtot, where Ctot and Dtot are the summed Backlog and Delay terms, and the slack as S = Dreq - (b/r + Ctot/r + Dtot). An element can use slack to admit flows that would otherwise be rejected.
sections.eli5: Backlog is how much stuff can pile up, Delay is the longest a packet might wait, and Slack is spare time that the router can use to ask for less of its resources.

sections.title: Status, Notifications and Conformance
sections.content:
intSrvGuaranteedIfStatus is a RowStatus column. It is valid on interfaces that are configured for the Guaranteed Service.

No notifications are defined. For conformance, the module has one compliance statement that makes the group intSrvGuaranteedIfAttribGroup mandatory. That group contains all four table columns and is required for systems supporting the Guaranteed Service of the Integrated Services Architecture.
sections.eli5: A switch tells whether each plug is set up for the guaranteed option. Anything that claims to support the option must have all four boxes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC notes one specific point: an SNMP SET results in an RSVP or Integrated Services reservation under rules that differ from those applied when the reservation is negotiated using RSVP. Beyond that, no security considerations exist other than those imposed by SNMP itself.
sections.eli5: Changing a setting by remote control makes a booking in a different way than asking nicely through the normal route. Otherwise it is as safe as the remote control itself.

references.text: Rose, M., Editor, "Management Information Base for Network Management of TCP/IP-based internets", STD 17, RFC 1213, May 1990.
